title: Collecting debt can mark more paid than bank confirmed
simple: When the desk presses "Collect what's owed" for a patient, the system settles every unpaid bill that patient has, not only the ones shown on screen. If the payment is a bank transfer, the amount the bank confirmed is never compared with the total being marked paid.
example: Almaz owes 1,200 birr from last month and 300 birr today. She sends a 300 birr transfer and the bank check confirms 300. Hana at reception presses Collect; all 1,500 birr is marked paid against that one 300 birr transfer.
why: The clinic records 1,200 birr as received that never arrived, and the debt disappears from every report.
fix: Reception will only settle the exact bills it showed, and a transfer will be refused if the bank-confirmed amount is less than the total being settled.

log.note: Explained; owner said fix it (no manager override). Built: a settlement can never exceed the amount the bank confirmed for its reference (code AMOUNT_EXCEEDS_VERIFIED, refused whole, nothing marked paid, reference stays free); one rule in ClaimReference covers the whole-visit, single-charge and pharmacy doors; a reference with no bank answer is not compared. Live check beforehand: no payment had settled above its confirmed amount. Full run in progress.

title: Cash day close splits days at 3 a.m. Addis
simple: The cashier's day close (Z-report) and the list of days split the day at midnight UTC, which is 3 a.m. in Addis. Money taken between midnight and 3 a.m. Addis is filed under the previous day.
example: Selam closes the 16th at 23:30 with 8,000 birr counted. At 00:16 on the 17th an emergency patient pays 1,500 birr. That 1,500 lands in the 16th, which is already closed, so the 16th now looks 1,500 short of what was counted and the 17th looks 1,500 over.
why: Drawer counts never match, so real shortages are hidden among false ones and staff may be wrongly blamed.
fix: Every day boundary in billing will be midnight Addis time, the same as the Finance screens already use.

title: Home screen ignores refunds made today
simple: When a payment is refunded, the refund is saved without the branch it belongs to. The home screen counts money per branch, so it never subtracts the refund, while the Finance page does.
example: Today the clinic took 10,000 birr and refunded 2,000 birr to Tigist. The home screen says 10,000 birr collected; Finance says 8,000.
why: The owner sees more money than the clinic actually kept, and two screens disagree about the same day.
fix: Refunds will carry the branch of the original payment (old refunds fixed too), so every screen shows the same net figure.

title: Manager override of a rejected transfer keeps no reason
simple: If the bank says a transfer is wrong (for example it went to another account), only a manager can force it through, and the screen asks for a reason. That reason, and who gave it, is never saved anywhere.
example: The bank check says Abebe's 900 birr transfer went to a different account. Manager Meron forces it through, typing "patient showed bank SMS". Next month the money is missing and nobody can see who approved it or why.
why: A decision to accept a payment the bank disputed leaves no trace, so a mistake or fraud cannot be traced.
fix: Store the manager's name and reason with the payment, and show it in the audit log.

title: Two desks pressing at once charge the registration fee twice
simple: When a patient arrives, the system checks whether today's registration fee already exists and then adds it. If two staff press at the same moment, both see "none yet" and both add one.
example: Hana and the manager both receive Almaz at the same moment. Almaz now has two 200 birr registration fees waiting at the cashier, and she cannot be queued until both are cleared.
why: Patients are overcharged or held at the door, and cashiers must spot and void the duplicate by hand.
fix: Make the fee check and the fee creation one locked step, so only one fee per patient per day can ever exist.

log.note: Fixed as part of FEAT-REG-1: the arrival decision holds the patient's row, so simultaneous arrivals raise one fee. The known-bug test is now a plain test (passed 3 runs in a row).

title: Branch cashiers see and handle other branches' bills
simple: A cashier or manager set up for one branch can see the other branch's waiting bills, and can take payment for, void, waive or refund them. A branch manager can also open the other branch's money figures in Finance just by choosing it.
example: Selam works only at the Bole branch. On her list she sees a 400 birr bill from the Piassa branch, and she can mark it paid or write it off. The Bole manager can read Piassa's takings for the day.
why: Money can be moved or forgiven at a branch the person does not work at, and branch figures are visible to staff who should not see them.
fix: Every money screen and money action will check the person's own branches, refusing anything at a branch they are not assigned to.

title: Staff can work in branches not assigned to them
simple: The system knows which branch each staff member belongs to, but never checks it when they do something. A receptionist from one branch can book patients, add them to the queue, move queue patients or raise bills at another branch.
example: Hana works only at Bole. She books a patient into Piassa's diary, puts a walk-in into Piassa's queue, and adds a 50 birr bill under Piassa. All are accepted.
why: Branch limits the owner sets do nothing; bills and bookings can appear in the wrong branch's books and diary.
fix: Check the person's branches on every booking, queue and billing action, and refuse other branches.

title: Re-closing wipes first count; refunds hit wrong drawer
simple: If a cashier closes the same day twice, the second count replaces the first, so an earlier shortage disappears. Also, when a manager refunds cash a cashier took, the refund is taken out of the manager's drawer instead of the cashier's.
example: Selam closes at 690 birr against 700 expected (10 short). Later she closes again at 700, and the 10 birr shortage is gone from the record. Separately, Selam took 500 birr; manager Meron refunds it in cash. Selam's drawer is still expected to hold 500 and Meron's shows minus 500.
why: Shortages can be erased after the fact, and drawer totals are wrong for both people.
fix: Keep every close as its own record (the latest shown, earlier ones kept), and take a refund out of the drawer that took the money.
decision: When a manager refunds cash, whose drawer should the money come out of: the cashier who took it, or the person handing it back?

title: Finance shows too little owed when dental figures fail
simple: If the part of the system that adds up dental treatment money fails, the Finance debt page quietly leaves it out instead of showing an error.
example: Patients owe 300 birr at the cashier and 1,000 birr of dental work not yet billed. A hiccup in the dental figures makes Finance say 300 birr owed, with no warning.
why: The owner makes decisions on a debt figure that is silently too low.
fix: Show an error when any part of the money figure cannot be read, never a partial total.

title: Old card-fee button can take money Finance never sees
simple: An old way of taking a card fee still works behind the scenes. Money taken that way is kept in a separate old list and never appears in Finance or the day close. No screen uses it today, but it can still be called.
example: Someone uses the old card-fee route to take 150 birr from a patient. Finance shows 0 birr collected for it and the drawer does not expect it.
why: Money can be taken outside the books, where no report or day close will catch it.
fix: Remove the old card-fee route (or send its money through the normal billing records).

title: A listed service can be billed at any price
simple: When staff add a service from the price list, the system uses the price sent with the request instead of the price list. The normal screens send the right price, but anyone who can raise bills could send a different one.
example: The price list says a panoramic X-ray is 1,500 birr. A bill is raised for it with the price set to 1 birr, and it is saved at 1 birr.
why: The price list can be bypassed, so services can be sold for almost nothing without anyone approving a discount.
fix: When a price-list service is named, always use the price list's amount; discounts go through the waive/forgive steps that need a reason.

title: "Paid today" list starts at 3 a.m., not midnight
simple: The cashier's "Paid today" list starts at midnight UTC (3 a.m. Addis). Payments taken between midnight and 3 a.m. are missing; between midnight and 3 a.m. it shows yesterday afternoon's payments instead.
example: Selam takes 450 birr at 00:30. When she opens "Paid today" to reprint the receipt, it is not there.
why: Cashiers cannot find or reprint early-morning receipts and may think a payment was lost.
fix: Start "Paid today" at midnight Addis time.

title: Early-morning arrivals can get a second registration fee
simple: To avoid charging the registration fee twice in one day, the system looks for a fee raised "today". Because of a time-zone slip, "today" starts at 6 a.m. Addis, so a fee raised before 6 a.m. is not found.
example: Almaz is received at 05:30 and a 200 birr fee is raised. At 05:45 the desk presses receive again; a second 200 birr fee is added.
why: Patients arriving before 6 a.m. can be charged twice. Most clinics are closed then, so it is rare.
fix: Make "today" start at midnight Addis time for this check.

log.note: Confirmed live in the night window: the 'today' cut-off is 06:00 Addis, so every check-in from 00:00 to 06:00 can raise the fee again (TestREG_BILL_080 now reports it as this bug in that window).
Raised from medium to high: from 00:00 to 06:00 Addis every check-in can charge the registration fee again.

title: Receptionist can make any visit free as a follow-up
simple: The clinic rule is that only a follow-up booked by the doctor is free. Today the system only checks the "follow-up" tick and the end date, so a booking the receptionist ticks as a follow-up is also free.
example: Hana books Abebe as a follow-up, or ticks "follow-up" on his ordinary booking. When he arrives, no 200 birr fee is raised.
why: Fees can be skipped without a doctor's decision, and the lost money is never recorded as a discount.
fix: Make a visit free only when a doctor ordered the follow-up; desk-made follow-ups pay the normal fee.
decision: Should a receptionist ever book a free follow-up for the doctor (for example when the doctor asks by phone), or must the doctor always book it?

title: Cancelled or no-show follow-ups still check in free
simple: A follow-up that was cancelled or marked no-show should no longer give a free visit. But check-in changes the booking to "arrived" before the fee rule looks at it, so the rule never sees it was cancelled.
example: Dr. Dawit books Tigist a free follow-up. She cancels. Two days later she walks in and the desk checks in the cancelled booking: no fee is charged.
why: Free visits are given for bookings that did not happen, so fees are lost.
fix: Refuse check-in of a cancelled or no-show booking (or charge the fee), by reading the status before changing it.

title: Patient charged on the last day of free follow-up
simple: The booking screen promises "free if attended on or before" a date. The fee rule treats that date as ending at its first minute (midnight), so a patient who comes later that same day is charged.
example: Abebe's follow-up is "free until 10 October". He comes at 10:00 on 10 October and is asked for 200 birr.
why: Patients are charged against what the clinic promised them, causing arguments at the desk.
fix: Count the free window to the end of its last day, Addis time.

title: Any cashier can see every cashier's day closes
simple: The list of all cashiers' day closes is meant for managers. A plain cashier can get it too by asking for "all".
example: Selam can see how much Meron counted each day and whether Meron was short.
why: Colleagues can see each other's shortages; this is meant to be a manager-only view.
fix: Return only the cashier's own closes unless the person has the manager billing permission.

title: "Open drawers" misses money taken just after midnight
simple: On the Finance cash tab, the "open drawers" figure (money cashiers hold but have not closed) uses the UTC day. Money taken between midnight and 3 a.m. Addis is left out. (The audit calls this FIN-11.)
example: Selam took 700 birr during the day and 40 birr at 00:30. The by-cashier line says 740 birr; her open drawer says 700.
why: The owner sees less cash in hand than the cashier really holds.
fix: Use the Addis day for open drawers, the same as the rest of the tab.

title: A pharmacy payment reference can be used again
simple: Each bank or Telebirr payment reference should pay only once. When a reference is used for an over-the-counter pharmacy sale, no receipt number is saved with it, so the system treats it as unused and accepts it again.
example: A 300 birr Telebirr reference pays for a pharmacy sale. Later the same reference is entered for a clinic bill, and it is accepted.
why: One payment can settle two bills, so the clinic loses money. This only matters where the pharmacy is switched on.
fix: Treat any reference already used, with or without a receipt number, as spent.

title: Same Telebirr payment accepted twice through two accounts
simple: A payment reference is only checked against the payment method it was entered under. If the clinic has two Telebirr numbers set up, one real payment can be entered once under each.
example: Abebe pays 500 birr by Telebirr. Selam enters the reference under "Telebirr 1" for one bill; later it is entered under "Telebirr 2" for another 500 birr bill. Both are accepted.
why: One payment settles two bills, so 500 birr is lost.
fix: Make a reference unique per payment provider (all Telebirr numbers together), not per method entry.

log.note: Owner confirmed option A (by source). Built in ClaimReference: a reference that already paid a receipt is refused under any method of the same source (two numbers of one provider; a generic bank/mobile method beside any named one of its kind); different named providers and a wallet beside a bank stay separate; a row that was only checked is not use; claims on one reference are serialised by a lock so simultaneous desks cannot both win. The old insert-race fallback is gone with the race. Live check beforehand: no clinic had two methods of one provider, no reference under two methods; Joy Speciality has a generic bank beside CBE and Zemen (the real exposure). Full run in progress.

title: Bank check passes a payment when amount is missing
simple: When the payment-check service confirms a receipt but does not say how much it was for, the system skips the amount check and accepts the payment.
example: Almaz shows a transfer reference for a 1,000 birr bill. The check service says "verified" but gives no amount (the real transfer was 100 birr). The system accepts it as full payment.
why: A small transfer can be accepted as payment for a large bill.
fix: If the amount is missing, send the payment to manual review instead of accepting it.

log.note: Explained; owner agreed. Built: when an expected amount is given and the bank gave none (absent, null, or blank) the verdict is review ("did not say how much this was for"), never verified; no expected amount still skips the gate. Live check: the one bank-confirmed payment had an amount. Same full run as NEW-KERNEL-PAY-2.

title: Re-pricing a cancelled visit pushes its fee onto others
simple: When a visit in a treatment course is cancelled, the course total drops. If someone then re-prices that cancelled visit and chooses to spread the difference, its old fee is spread onto the remaining visits.
example: Selam's 3-visit course is 3,000 birr. Visit 1 is cancelled, so the course is 2,000 birr. Re-pricing visit 1 to 0 with "spread" moves the course back to 3,000 birr and visit 2 becomes 1,500 birr.
why: The patient is quoted 1,000 birr more than the course they agreed to.
fix: Refuse re-pricing of a cancelled visit.

title: "Pay later" can be set on paid or cancelled visits
simple: The "pay later" promise can be put on a dental visit that is already paid, already waiting at the cashier, or cancelled. Nothing checks the visit's state.
example: Dr. Dawit marks a cancelled visit for Tigist as "pay later, next month". It now shows as a promised visit even though it will never happen.
why: Screens show promises to pay for visits that are settled or will never happen, confusing staff about who owes what.
fix: Allow "pay later" only on a visit that is still owed (not paid, not at the cashier, not cancelled).

title: Chair list counts extras as treatment visits
simple: On the dentist's chair list, "visits done" counts extras (such as an X-ray added to a visit) as if they were visits, while the total counts only real visits.
example: Hana's course has 3 visits. Visit 1 is done with an X-ray added. The chair list says "2 of 3" instead of "1 of 3".
why: The dentist may think the course is further along than it is. No money changes.
fix: Count only real visits in the "done" number.

title: A given extra can be deleted with no reason
simple: An extra (for example an extraction added to a visit) that was done but not yet billed can be removed by any dentist, with no reason and no permission check. Visits have this protection; extras do not.
example: Dr. Dawit does a 2,000 birr extraction as an extra. Before it is billed, another dentist removes it. The debt and the record of the procedure both disappear.
why: Owed money and a clinical record can vanish without trace.
fix: Treat removing a done extra like forgiving owed treatment: same-day author or a manager, with a reason, and cancel it rather than delete it.

title: Price cuts and "pay later" leave no logged reason
simple: When a dentist changes a visit's price, the reason they type is not kept in the activity log. Marking a visit "pay later" leaves no log entry at all.
example: Dr. Dawit lowers a visit from 1,500 to 1,000 birr, typing "extra canal found", and marks another visit "pay later". The log shows a price change with no reason and nothing about pay later.
why: The owner cannot see why money was reduced or who agreed to wait for it.
fix: Save the reason with each price change, and record every pay-later decision with who, when and the note.

title: Deleting a patient hides what they owe
simple: A receptionist can delete a patient who still owes money. After that, the debt disappears from the Finance debt list, although the unpaid bill is still in the system.
example: Abebe owes 400 birr. Hana deletes his record. Finance no longer shows him or his 400 birr.
why: Debts can disappear from the owner's view, by mistake or on purpose.
fix: Refuse to delete a patient who owes money (or keep their debt visible in Finance).
decision: Should a patient with unpaid bills be impossible to delete, or deletable with their debt still shown?

title: Finance page says "Loading..." forever when it fails
simple: If the Finance page cannot load (no permission, server error, no internet), it shows "Loading..." for ever instead of an error.
example: The internet drops while the owner opens Finance. The page sits on "Loading..." and never says anything is wrong.
why: The owner waits or reloads without knowing why, and cannot tell a slow page from a broken one.
fix: Show a clear "could not load" message with a retry button.

title: Failed price list load says "No services yet"
simple: If the price list cannot load, the page says "No services yet - add the ones your clinic bills for" instead of showing an error.
example: The connection drops while the manager opens Services. Seeing "No services yet", she starts typing the whole price list again.
why: Staff may create duplicate services and prices, so patients get billed from the wrong entry.
fix: Show an error with a retry button when the list fails to load.

title: Cashier screen shows yesterday as "today" after midnight
simple: On the cashier's day-close tab, "today" is worked out in UTC. Between midnight and 3 a.m. Addis, the screen labels yesterday as today.
example: At 01:30 on the 13th, Selam opens Day close. The row marked "today" is the 12th.
why: A cashier working late can close the wrong day.
fix: Work out "today" in Addis time on the cashier screen (part of the FIN-1 fix).

title: Reprinted Z-report shows the wrong cashier's name
simple: When an old day close (Z-report) is reprinted, it prints the name of whoever is signed in now, not the cashier who actually closed that day.
example: Meron closed 1 October with 800 birr. On 3 October Selam reprints it; the paper says "Selam" over Meron's count.
why: The printed record names the wrong person as responsible for the drawer.
fix: Print the name saved with the close, as receipt reprints already do.

title: Cancelled void/waive reason stays picked for the next bill
simple: If a cashier opens "Void" or "Waive" on a bill, picks a reason and then cancels, the next bill's Void/Waive box opens with that reason already chosen and the button ready to press.
example: Selam opens Waive on Abebe's bill, picks "Staff benefit", then cancels. She opens Waive on Almaz's bill; "Staff benefit" is already chosen and one click writes it off.
why: A bill can be voided or written off with the wrong reason by a quick click.
fix: Clear the reason every time the box is closed.

title: Patient payment history puts after-midnight payments on the wrong day
simple: In a patient's payment history and printed statement, payments are grouped by the UTC date. A payment taken between midnight and 3 a.m. Addis shows under the previous day.
example: Tigist pays at 00:30 on 3 October. Her statement lists it under 2 October.
why: The patient's statement shows a wrong date, which can cause questions.
fix: Group the history by Addis date.

title: "Pay later" at reception defers old debt, skips check-in
simple: At reception, "Pay later" should check the patient in and postpone only today's fee. Instead it does not check them in or raise today's fee, and it postpones every unpaid bill the patient has, including old ones and deposits.
example: Almaz owes 300 birr from last month and arrives for a visit with a 200 birr fee. The manager presses Pay later. Her old 300 birr is marked as agreed to pay later, today's 200 birr fee is never raised, and her booking is not marked arrived.
why: Today's fee is never charged, old debt is quietly turned into an agreed delay, and the booking looks missed.
fix: Make Pay later check the patient in first and postpone only the bills that this arrival raised.
decision: When a patient is let through on 'pay later', should only today's charges be deferred (recommended), or may the desk also defer older debts in the same step?

log.note: Fixed with the reception redesign (phase 2). Pay later now checks the patient in first and defers ONLY the charges that arrival raised; older debts are not quietly agreed to be waited for. Test REG-FE-RECEP-038 flipped from known-bug to a plain test; REG-FE-RECEP-054 covers the free-visit case. Full run green.

title: "To settle" patient offered a new visit, not their debt
simple: On reception's "To settle" list, opening a patient who owes money after their visit shows "nothing more to collect" and offers to start a new visit with a new fee, instead of letting the desk take what they owe.
example: Dawit's visit is finished and he owes 800 birr. Hana opens him from "To settle"; the panel offers a fresh 100 birr visit and no button to collect the 800.
why: Patients leave without paying, or are charged for a visit they did not ask for.
fix: For a patient on "To settle", show what they owe with a Collect button.

log.note: Fixed with the reception redesign (phase 2). A patient seen today who still owes now opens on a Collect button for what they owe, with 'Or start a new visit' beneath; the old 'nothing more to collect' line is gone. REG-FE-RECEP-039 flipped to a plain test. Full run green.

title: Desk without collect permission still sees "Collect" button
simple: A receptionist who is not allowed to take money still sees "Collect ... & send through". Pressing it checks the patient in and raises the fee, then the payment step is refused and an error shows.
example: Hana may raise bills but not take money. She presses "Collect 200 birr & send through" for Almaz; Almaz is checked in with a bill, but the screen shows an error.
why: Staff are confused about whether the patient paid, and may take cash with nothing recording it.
fix: Show "Send to cashier" as the main button for staff who cannot collect.

log.note: Fixed with the reception redesign (phase 2). A desk without payment.collect is offered 'Send to cashier' (with the total) as its only exit, never 'Collect'. REG-FE-RECEP-040 flipped to a plain test; REG-FE-RECEP-051 added. Full run green.

title: Retrying Collect at reception bills extras twice
simple: If a payment at reception fails (for example the transfer check refuses it) and the desk presses Collect again, any extra services chosen are billed a second time. The first set stays unpaid, which also keeps the patient out of the dentist's queue.
example: Hana adds a 300 birr X-ray for Abebe. The first Collect is refused by the bank check; she presses again with cash. A second X-ray bill is raised and paid; the first stays unpaid, so Abebe never appears in the dentist's queue.
why: The patient owes twice for one service and can be stuck at the door unseen.
fix: Raise extras only once per arrival (reuse the first attempt's bills on retry).

log.note: Explained. Owner decided reception does not need "Add a service" (no clinic uses it; discuss again if one asks). Removed it from the reception page: the section, its tick boxes, the "Added services" line and the request that raised each extra. With no extras raised at reception there is nothing to bill twice. Only the arrival fee is raised, which the server already hands back on a repeat press. The server capability is untouched; if the feature returns, it must be built as one all-or-nothing receive action. REG-FE-RECEP-018 now asserts no extra is raised. Frontend checks green (lint, types, 1,644 screen tests with minimums, 10 of 10 journeys); no server change. Not yet deployed.

title: A single bill cannot be part-paid
simple: A bill is either paid in full or not at all. Paying in parts only works if a deposit and visits were agreed in advance on a treatment course.
example: Almaz's bill today is 3,250 birr; she can pay 1,000 now. The cashier cannot record the 1,000 against it.
why: Cashiers keep part-payments outside the system or turn patients away, so records and cash drift apart.
fix: Allow recording a part-payment against a bill, leaving the rest owed.
decision: Should cashiers be able to take part-payments on any bill, and should that need a manager's approval?

title: Down payment can be set to zero unchecked
simple: The down payment on a dental course can have its amount changed to 0 through the system, with no reason or permission check. The normal screens do not offer this, but nothing stops it.
example: Tigist's course has a 1,000 birr unpaid down payment. A change sets it to 0 and the 1,000 birr owed disappears.
why: Owed money can be forgiven with no reason or record of who did it.
fix: Treat lowering an unpaid down payment like any other forgiveness: a reason and the right permission.

title: "Finish treatment" strands visits the patient already paid for
simple: When a dentist finishes a course early, visits the patient already paid for but did not receive stay open inside a closed course. The finish dialog says everything is done.
example: Hana paid ahead for visits 3 and 4 (2,000 birr). The dentist finishes the course after visit 2. Visits 3 and 4 stay as paid, never given, and nothing prompts a refund or credit.
why: The patient's prepaid money is left in limbo; the clinic may owe a refund nobody sees.
fix: Warn about prepaid visits when finishing, and offer a refund or credit.
decision: When a course ends early, should prepaid visits be refunded, kept as credit, or left for the owner to decide each time?

title: Day list compares all-method takings with a cash-only count
simple: The list of days shows total takings from all payment methods next to a difference worked out from cash only, so the numbers look like they do not add up.
example: A day has 5,000 birr cash and 3,000 birr Telebirr. The row shows 8,000 taken beside a cash difference based on 5,000.
why: Owners may think a drawer is short when it is not.
fix: Label the columns clearly or show cash takings beside the cash count.

title: Pharmacy counter sales are kept outside the main books
simple: Over-the-counter pharmacy sales are stored separately from other bills. Only matters if the pharmacy module is switched on, which dental clinics do not use.
example: A clinic with the pharmacy on sells 500 birr of medicine over the counter; that money is handled outside the normal billing records.
why: Reports and day closes can miss pharmacy money where the pharmacy is used.
fix: Record counter sales as normal bills.

title: Old card-fee "paid today" uses the UTC day
simple: The old card-fee feature works out "paid today" by UTC. No screen uses it now; it goes away when the old card-fee route (FIN-13) is removed.
example: A card fee paid at 01:00 Addis is counted as yesterday's.
why: Minor: only affects the old, unused card-fee feature.
fix: Remove with FIN-13.

title: Removed staff keep access for up to a month
simple: When the owner deactivates or suspends a staff member, only new sign-ins are blocked. A phone or computer that was already signed in keeps renewing itself quietly and keeps full access for up to 30 days. Worse, an old password-reset link they still hold switches their account back on.
example: Selam the receptionist is let go on Monday and Hanna (owner) clicks Deactivate. Selam's phone is still signed in: for the next weeks she can open patient files, phone numbers and balances from home. She also kept a reset link from last month; opening it turns her account active again.
why: Someone the clinic has deliberately locked out can still read patient records and take actions in the clinic's name.
fix: When a staff member is deactivated or suspended, sign them out on every device at once and cancel their open invite and reset links; the renewal step will also check the account is still active.

title: Clinic's only owner can be demoted, suspended or removed
simple: Nothing protects the clinic's last owner. The owner can take away her own owner role by mistake, and a clinic administrator can demote, deactivate or delete the owner. Deleting yourself is blocked, but these other paths are not.
example: Dawit, the clinic administrator, edits staff roles and changes Hanna (the only owner) to receptionist. Hanna can no longer see Finance, settings or staff, and nobody in the clinic can give her owner rights back.
why: The clinic can lose the one person allowed to manage money, staff and settings, and needs the vendor to step in to restore it.
fix: Refuse any role change, suspension or removal that would leave the clinic with no active owner, with a clear message.
decision: Should a clinic administrator be allowed to change or remove the owner at all, or only the owner herself?

title: Owner can suspend herself and lock the clinic out
simple: The staff page hides the Delete button on your own row, but the Suspend button is still there, and the server accepts it. If the only owner suspends herself she is signed out and cannot get back in.
example: Hanna is tidying the staff list on her phone and taps Suspend on the wrong row, her own. She is thrown out and her password no longer works; the clinic has no one who can switch her back on until the vendor does it.
why: One mis-tap locks the clinic out of its own management screens until support intervenes.
fix: Hide Suspend on your own row and have the server refuse a self-suspension, the same way it already refuses deleting yourself.

title: Super-admin login can be guessed forever, no lockout
simple: The platform (vendor) sign-in has no limit on wrong passwords and no second step like a phone code. Someone can try passwords endlessly; after ten wrong tries the right one still works.
example: An attacker runs a password list against the platform login overnight. When it hits the right password they can open every clinic, change plans, suspend clinics, or sign in as any clinic owner.
why: One guessed password exposes every clinic's patients and money at once.
fix: Lock the platform account for a while after a few failed tries, add a phone-app code (two-step sign-in) for platform admins, and optionally allow platform login only from known addresses.

title: "Sign in as owner" leaves no trace of who acted
simple: When a platform admin uses "Sign in as owner" to help a clinic, the clinic's history does not record it. Everything done in that session looks exactly as if the owner did it herself.
example: While helping Cure Dental, a support person waives a 3,000 birr charge. The clinic's history says Hanna (owner) waived it; she insists she never did and nobody can show otherwise.
why: Actions taken by vendor staff inside a clinic cannot be told apart from the owner's own, which breaks trust and accountability.
fix: Write a history entry naming the platform admin whenever they sign in as an owner, and mark that session so every action in it is recorded as "done by support on behalf of the owner".

title: A file record can point at another clinic's stored file
simple: After a file is uploaded, the app tells the server where the file is stored, and the server believes it. It does not check that the location belongs to this clinic and this patient, or that the chosen visit belongs to this patient. Opening the record then gives a link to that file, and deleting it deletes that file.
example: A staff member at Clinic A who somehow learns the storage location of an X-ray at Clinic B records it on one of her own patients. She can now view Clinic B's X-ray, and pressing Delete erases it from Clinic B too. In the same way an X-ray can be filed on a different patient's visit or on the down payment.
why: Another clinic's patient files could be read or destroyed. The locations contain long random codes, which makes this hard to exploit, but it should not depend on that.
fix: Only accept a storage location that sits in this clinic's own folder for this patient (or have the server hand out the location itself), and check that the chosen visit belongs to the same patient.

title: Busy moments can block every clinic with "too many requests"
simple: The system limits how many requests can come in per second, to protect itself. But it counts before it knows who is asking, and behind Cloudflare almost everyone appears to come from the same few addresses. So all users of all clinics can end up sharing one small allowance of about 20 requests a second.
example: At 9:00 Cure Dental's reception, cashier and two dentists all have dashboards and queue screens refreshing, while Bole Dental opens for the day. Requests pile up and staff at both clinics start seeing "too many requests" errors and blank screens for a few seconds at a time.
why: Ordinary daily use can be refused at the busiest moments, and one busy clinic can slow down another. Login records also store Cloudflare's address instead of the real one.
fix: Read the real visitor address from Cloudflare, count requests per signed-in user after sign-in, and keep a strict limit only on the sign-in pages.
decision: Check the live server's access logs first to confirm how often this happens today.

title: Cashier can watch the live queue she should not see
simple: The live queue feed (who has arrived, who is waiting, who is with the doctor) only checks that you are signed in. A cashier, who is not allowed to open the queue board, can still receive the live feed. Each open feed also holds a database connection with no limit.
example: Meron the cashier opens the queue feed link and sees every arriving patient's name and which doctor they are waiting for, although her role was set up not to see the queue. If many tabs open the feed, the server can run short of database connections.
why: Staff see information their role was meant to hide, and many open feeds can slow the whole system.
fix: Require the same queue permission for the live feed as for the queue board, and share one database connection between all feeds.

title: Front desk sees empty X-ray list, not "not allowed"
simple: Reception and cashier are allowed onto the dental image list but the server quietly empties it for them, so no X-ray is actually shown. It works, but the screen reads "no images" rather than "you don't have access", and the protection depends on that one emptying step. They can still see the tooth chart, by design.
example: Selam at reception opens Abebe's X-rays to check one is there before his visit. The list says there are none, although the dentist uploaded two yesterday; she tells the patient to bring his X-ray again.
why: Misleading to front-desk staff, and a weaker protection than a plain refusal.
fix: Refuse the image list outright for roles without clinical access, and show a "clinical staff only" message on screen.
decision: Should reception and cashier see the tooth chart and the image count at all, or nothing clinical?

title: Writes aimed at another clinic's record are accepted silently
simple: If a request names a patient, branch, allergen or staff member that belongs to a different clinic, the server still saves the new item, inside the requesting clinic, pointing at something it cannot see. The other clinic sees nothing and nothing leaks, but the request is told "saved".
example: A faulty link at Clinic A adds a "Penicillin - severe" allergy using a patient number from Clinic B. Clinic B's patient is unchanged, but Clinic A now holds an orphan allergy record and the screen said "Saved". The same happens for conditions, guardians, attachments, certificates, history imports, department branches, drug allergy tags and staff roles.
why: Junk records build up that belong to no visible patient, and "saved" versus "not found" answers reveal that a given record number exists in some clinic.
fix: Check that the named patient, branch, allergen or staff member belongs to the same clinic before saving, and answer "not found" otherwise; add database rules that enforce it.

title: Dental records can be saved against another clinic's patient
simple: The dental chart, treatment plans, medical history and images accept a patient number from another clinic. The record is stored in the requesting clinic, pointing at a patient it cannot see. The other clinic's patient is untouched and nothing is shown across clinics.
example: A dentist at Clinic B, using a wrong link, saves "UR6 extracted" and a 1,000 birr plan on a patient number from Clinic A. Clinic A sees no change, but Clinic B now has a chart and a plan for a patient who does not exist for it, and the answer differed from a made-up number, which reveals that the number is real.
why: Orphan dental records and a way to test whether a patient number exists somewhere.
fix: Before saving any dental record, confirm the patient belongs to this clinic and answer "not found" otherwise.

title: Branch module switches answer "saved" for another clinic's branch
simple: Reading or changing which modules are on for a branch does not check the branch is yours. Asking about another clinic's branch returns your own defaults, and changing it stores a stray setting in your clinic. The other clinic is not affected.
example: Through a bad link, Hanna turns off Dental for a branch number that belongs to another clinic. The screen says saved; nothing changes anywhere that matters, but a stray setting sits in Cure Dental's data.
why: A misleading success message and leftover junk settings.
fix: Answer "branch not found" unless the branch belongs to the clinic.

title: Renaming or deleting a missing department says "done"
simple: Renaming or deleting a department that does not exist (or belongs to another clinic) answers as if it worked. Nothing actually changes.
example: Two managers edit departments at the same time; one deletes "Hygiene" and the other renames it a second later. The rename says saved, but the department is gone.
why: The person is told a change was saved when it was not.
fix: Answer "department not found" when nothing was changed.

title: Editing a deleted drug or allergen says "saved"
simple: Editing or removing a drug or allergen that no longer exists answers as if it worked. Nothing is changed.
example: Dr Selam renames "Amoxicillin 500mg" in one tab after a colleague already removed it in another. The screen says saved, but the drug list does not have it.
why: A false "saved" message; the person does not learn the item is gone.
fix: Answer "not found" when no drug or allergen was changed.

title: Internal "no clinic" lookups error instead of finding nothing
simple: The database protection that keeps clinics apart is working and stays locked. But in one rare internal situation (a lookup with no clinic set, on a reused connection) it throws an error instead of simply returning nothing.
example: A background job that runs a lookup without a clinic set occasionally fails with a confusing error instead of quietly finding no rows. No patient data is shown anywhere.
why: Confusing failures in background work; no data exposure.
fix: Adjust the database protection rules so an empty clinic setting means "no rows", not an error.

title: Branch reception hears the other branch's live queue
simple: The live queue feed sends every arrival in the clinic to every open screen, whichever branch the person works at. A receptionist limited to one branch sees the other branch's patients arriving. The feed also carries the sign-in pass in the web address.
example: Cure Dental opens a second site in Piassa. Selam, who works only at Bole, sees "Abebe Kebede checked in" pop up for the Piassa branch on her queue board.
why: Branch staff see patients who are not theirs. Matters only once a clinic has a second branch.
fix: Send each queue event only to people allowed at that branch.

title: Dental calendar shows visits from another branch
simple: The dental visits calendar is not filtered by branch, unlike the appointment diary beside it. A desk limited to branch A sees visits delivered at branch B.
example: At a clinic with Bole and Piassa branches, the Bole desk opens the dental calendar and sees a root canal done at Piassa today mixed in with Bole's visits.
why: Branch staff see other branches' patients, and the two calendars disagree. Matters only once a clinic has a second branch.
fix: Filter the dental calendar by the branches the person may see, like the appointment diary.

title: Branch screen shows plan's cap, not the clinic's real one
simple: When you give a clinic its own branch limit (different from its plan), the settings screen still shows the plan's limit. Adding a branch is then refused although the screen said there was room.
example: Bole Dental is on the 10-branch plan but you set it to 1 branch. Their settings page says "1 of 10 branches" and offers "Add branch"; Hanna fills in the Piassa branch and gets "branch limit reached".
why: Confusing screen that promises something the server will refuse.
fix: Show the limit the server actually enforces, including the clinic's own override.

title: Removed staff email or deleted branch code is blocked forever
simple: When a staff member is removed, their email is still treated as taken, so they can never be invited back to the same clinic. A deleted branch's short code is likewise blocked forever.
example: Nurse Tigist leaves in March and is removed. In June she returns; Hanna invites tigist@gmail.com and is told "email already taken", with no way to fix it.
why: Returning staff cannot be re-added without a new email address; branch codes are burned.
fix: Only count active (not removed) staff and branches when checking for duplicates.

title: Staff invites, suspensions and role changes are not recorded
simple: Inviting a staff member, suspending one or changing their role leaves no entry in the clinic's history. There is no record of who gave or took away access.
example: A receptionist suddenly has cashier rights and has been waiving charges. Hanna asks "who gave her that?" and the history has no answer.
why: Changes to who can do what in the clinic cannot be traced afterwards.
fix: Record every invite, status change and role change in the clinic's history, with who did it and what changed.

title: New branches, payment accounts and SMS settings are not recorded
simple: Opening a branch, adding a payment account (bank or Telebirr) or changing SMS settings leaves no entry in the clinic's history.
example: A new Telebirr account appears on the payment list and patients have been paying into it for a week. Nobody can tell who added it or when.
why: The question "who pointed our money to this account?" has no answer.
fix: Record branch, payment account and SMS settings changes in the clinic's history, with who and when.

title: Deleting a patient leaves no record of who did it
simple: When a patient record is deleted, nothing is written to the clinic's history. The record disappears and nobody can tell who removed it or when.
example: Almaz's file, with an unpaid 4,500 birr balance, is gone from the list on Monday. Three receptionists worked on Saturday; the history cannot say which one deleted it.
why: Records can vanish without any trace of who removed them.
fix: Record each patient deletion in the clinic's history with who did it, and ideally a reason.

title: A history entry can be written twice
simple: The clinic's history is written by a background worker. If the worker has to retry a step, the same entry can be written a second time.
example: The history shows "Hanna waived 500 birr" twice at 10:14, and the owner wonders whether two waivers happened.
why: Confusing duplicate history lines; no money is affected.
fix: Skip writing an entry that has already been written for the same event.

title: Files still save after a clinic's storage is full
simple: When a clinic's storage is full, the app refuses to start a new upload. But the final "save this file" step does not check again, so a request that skips the first step still saves files past the limit.
example: Bole Dental is on a 1 GB plan and full. A custom tool (or a retried request) records two more X-rays and a PDF, pushing them past 1 GB without being asked to upgrade.
why: Plan limits you sell can be bypassed; storage costs grow without payment.
fix: Check the storage limit again when the file is recorded, not only when the upload starts.

title: Retired plan can still be given to a new clinic
simple: A retired plan is meant to stay only for clinics already on it. But the "new clinic" form still offers it, and the server accepts it. Changing an existing clinic's plan already refuses retired plans.
example: You retired the old 1,500 birr "Legacy" plan. A colleague setting up a new clinic picks it from the list and the clinic is created on the old price.
why: New clinics can land on prices you no longer sell.
fix: Hide retired plans from the new-clinic form and refuse them on the server.

title: Usage page for a missing clinic shows a server error
simple: Asking for the usage of a clinic that does not exist returns a general server error instead of "clinic not found".
example: You open an old bookmark to a clinic you deleted in testing and get "Something went wrong" rather than "no such clinic".
why: Confusing error; no data affected.
fix: Answer "clinic not found".

title: Saving an unknown plan feature shows a server error
simple: Saving a plan with a feature name that is not in the feature list returns a general server error instead of "unknown feature".
example: An outdated console page sends a feature that was renamed; you get "Something went wrong" and do not know why.
why: Confusing error; nothing is saved.
fix: Check feature names against the list and say which one is unknown.

title: Suspending a whole clinic happens on one click, no question
simple: On the platform console the Suspend button locks a clinic out immediately, with no "are you sure?". "Sign in as owner" asks first, but Suspend does not.
example: Scrolling the clinic list on your phone you tap Suspend on Cure Dental instead of the test clinic below it. Their staff can no longer sign in in the middle of a busy morning.
why: One mis-tap stops a real clinic from working until someone notices and reactivates it.
fix: Ask for confirmation, naming the clinic, before suspending.

title: A failed load looks like "nothing here", not an error
simple: When a list fails to load (bad connection, server problem), several screens show the empty-state message instead of an error. Reception's patient search says "Nobody matches. Register them"; the cashier's day close looks like a quiet day; the platform console says "No clinics yet".
example: The internet drops for a moment. Selam searches "Abebe" and sees "Nobody matches. Register them", so she registers Abebe again, creating a duplicate file without his allergies or his 2,000 birr balance.
why: Staff act on a false "empty" picture: duplicate patients, wrong day-close checks, and needless worry.
fix: Show a clear "could not load, try again" message whenever a list fails, separate from the real empty state.

title: A refused change is not reported; the page says nothing
simple: Some admin buttons (suspend or reactivate a staff member, remove a drug or allergen, remove the receipt-check key on the platform) show nothing when the server refuses. The row stays as it was and the person assumes it worked.
example: Hanna suspends a dentist who has left; the server refuses because of a network hiccup. Nothing appears, Hanna assumes it worked, and the dentist keeps his access.
why: People believe a change was made when it was not, including changes about who can access the clinic.
fix: Show an error message whenever one of these actions is refused, saying why.

title: Half-filled new treatment plan lost on Esc or outside click
simple: The long "New treatment plan" form closes, and everything typed is thrown away, if you press Esc or click just outside it. There is no question first.
example: Dr Selam has typed a crown plan: 6,000 birr total, 1,500 down payment, three visits a week apart. Reaching for the mouse she clicks the grey area beside the form; it closes and she starts again with the patient waiting.
why: Wasted chair time and re-typing; a rushed second entry is more likely to contain mistakes.
fix: Keep the form open on Esc or outside clicks once something is typed, or ask "discard this plan?" first.

title: Two open tabs can sign everyone out without saying so
simple: Every so often the app quietly renews its sign-in. If two tabs (or a weak connection that retries) renew at the same moment, the server treats it as a stolen pass and signs that person out everywhere. The app does not then take them to the sign-in page; screens just show "could not load" errors.
example: Meron has Reception and Cashier open in two tabs. Both renew at 10:15 at once; she is signed out on every device. The pages fill with errors, and when she reloads to recover, the examination notes Dr Selam was typing on the shared computer are lost.
why: Sudden unexplained breakdowns in the middle of work, and lost unsaved notes.
fix: Let the server accept a just-replaced pass for a short moment, share the renewal between tabs, and when the session really ends show a sign-in box over the page instead of breaking it.

log.note: Half fixed with SEC-10: a session that dies mid-use now signs the app out and the sign-in page says so (REG-FE-SESSION-002 is now a normal test). Still open: two tabs refreshing at once can revoke each other.

title: An empty list from the server can crash a screen
simple: When the server answers "empty" in one particular way, the app mistakes the reply's wrapper for the list itself. A screen expecting a list then fails and shows a crash page instead of "nothing yet".
example: A new clinic opens a list that has never had any entries; instead of "No staff yet" the page goes blank with an error.
why: A white crash screen for something as normal as an empty list.
fix: Treat an empty answer as an empty list in the shared request code.

title: A damaged stored password makes sign-in crash
simple: If a stored password record were ever corrupted (for example by a bad manual database edit), signing in as that person crashes the request instead of saying "wrong password". The server recovers, but the person sees a general error.
example: After a manual data fix, Dr Selam's sign-in always shows "Something went wrong" and support cannot tell why.
why: A confusing failure for one account; rare.
fix: Check the stored password record is sane and treat a bad one as a failed sign-in.

title: A sign-in pass with no expiry date would be accepted
simple: The server accepts a correctly signed sign-in pass that has no expiry date at all. The server never makes such passes itself, so this needs the secret signing key to exploit; it is a safety-net gap.
example: If the signing key ever leaked, a pass made without an expiry would keep working forever instead of 15 minutes.
why: Removes one layer of protection if the signing key is ever exposed.
fix: Refuse any pass that has no expiry date.

title: "Too many requests" does not say when to try again
simple: When the server refuses because of too many requests, it does not say how long to wait. Screens that refresh automatically retry straight away and make it worse.
example: During the morning rush the queue screen gets "too many requests", retries at once, and keeps getting refused for longer than needed.
why: Slower recovery from busy moments.
fix: Include a "retry after N seconds" hint with the refusal and have the app respect it.

title: Monthly SMS allowance starts at 3 a.m., not midnight
simple: The monthly SMS count resets at midnight UTC, which is 3:00 a.m. in Addis. Messages sent between midnight and 3 a.m. on the 1st count toward the previous month.
example: A clinic's reminder batch goes out at 01:00 on 1 October; those 200 texts are counted in last month, which was already closed, so they are effectively free.
why: Small miscount of SMS usage at month boundaries.
fix: Start the SMS month at midnight Addis time.

title: File storage does not block "../" tricks in file names
simple: The storage layer would accept a file name containing "../" that steps out of the clinic's folder. Today the app always builds safe names itself, so this cannot be reached; it is a missing safety net.
example: If a future screen let the user name an upload, a name like "../../otherclinic/x" could land in another clinic's folder.
why: A future change could open a hole between clinics' files.
fix: Refuse any file name containing ".." in the storage layer.

title: PDFs on the backup storage service would not open
who: Clinics, only if storage falls back to Cloudinary
simple: The older Cloudinary storage option builds every link as if the file were an image. PDFs and other documents would get a link that does not work and could not be deleted. Production uses Cloudflare R2, so this only matters if the system falls back to Cloudinary.
example: R2 fails to start after a deploy, the app silently switches to Cloudinary, and a referral letter PDF uploaded that day will not open.
why: Broken document links in a fallback situation.
fix: Use the right document type when building Cloudinary links and deletions, or remove the fallback.
decision: Do you still want the Cloudinary fallback at all, now that R2 is live?

title: One clinic's broken time-zone setting stops SMS for every clinic
simple: The SMS sender and reminder planner handle all clinics in one go. If one clinic's time-zone setting were invalid, the whole run fails and no clinic's messages go out. Clinics cannot change this setting themselves today, so it would take a bad manual edit.
example: A typo in one clinic's time zone during a manual fix, and that evening no clinic sends any reminders.
why: One clinic's bad data can stop reminders for all clinics.
fix: Check the time zone per clinic and skip (and report) a clinic with an invalid one, letting the others continue.

title: Unsent SMS texts and patient phones written to server logs
simple: When SMS is not switched on, the system writes each message it would have sent, with the patient's phone number and the full text, into the server log.
example: The log contains "to 251911223344: Almaz, you owe 4,500 ETB for your root canal". Anyone who can read logs, or a log file copied for debugging, sees patient phone numbers, treatments and debts.
why: Patient health and money details end up in a place that is not protected like the database.
fix: Log only that a message was skipped, with a masked number and no text.

title: All backups sit on the same server as the database
simple: Backups are made every night, but they are kept only on the same server's disk, next to the database. The copy to a separate storage account is ready but switched off until a backup key is created. The secret keys needed to read some encrypted fields sit beside them. This is the one item the audit says blocks go-live.
example: The hosting company has a disk failure on a Sunday night. On Monday Cure Dental has no patient list, no balances owed, no treatment history, and no backup anywhere else to restore from.
why: Losing the one server means losing every patient record, payment and history for good.
fix: Create a separate backup storage account and key, encrypt the nightly backup and keys, upload them off the server every night, and do one test restore on another machine. Until then, copy the latest backup off the server daily by hand.

log.note: Walked through with the owner; waiting for confirmation and the backup key.

title: Backups and the secrets file are not encrypted
simple: The nightly database backup and the archive of server secrets are stored as plain files. Once they are copied off the server, anyone who gets that backup storage key can read every patient and every system password.
example: A backup storage key is accidentally pasted in a chat. Whoever finds it can download a full copy of all clinics' patients and the server's secret keys.
why: A single leaked key would expose all patient data and all production secrets.
fix: Encrypt both files before upload, with the unlock key kept off the server (password manager plus a printed copy).

title: No monitoring: problems are found when a clinic phones
simple: Nothing watches the system. If the server hangs, the background worker stops, the nightly backup fails or the disk fills, nobody is told. The "health" page always says up.
example: The backup has silently failed for nine days and the background worker stopped sending reminders. You find out when Cure Dental calls asking why patients stopped getting texts.
why: Outages and failed backups go unnoticed for days.
fix: Add an outside uptime check on the readiness page, a "backup succeeded" check-in alert, health checks for the API and worker, and a disk-space alert.

title: No written, tested way to restore a backup
simple: A restore has been done once, by hand. There is no script or step-by-step guide, so after a disaster someone must work out the steps under pressure on live data.
example: At 2 a.m. a bad update damages the database. You must stop the system, rebuild the database and its access account, restore, and check counts, while clinics open in six hours, all from memory.
why: Slow, error-prone recovery exactly when it matters most.
fix: Write a restore script that by default restores into a throwaway copy and checks counts, practise it monthly, and note how long it takes.

title: X-rays and uploaded files have no backup
simple: The nightly backup covers the database only. X-rays, photos and documents live in Cloudflare R2 with no second copy, and the app's own key can delete them. If R2 fails to start, the system silently switches to another storage or to none.
example: A bug or a stolen app key deletes the files folder. All patients' X-rays are gone; the database still lists them but the images do not open.
why: Clinical images could be lost permanently.
fix: Turn on deletion protection or retention on the files bucket, or copy it nightly to the backup storage, and refuse to start without R2 in production.

log.note: Deleting an image no longer destroys the stored file (see DEN-2), which removes the main way files were lost. Files still have no second copy.

title: Server door 8443 is open to the internet, bypassing Cloudflare
simple: The server accepts connections from anywhere on its back door (port 8443), not only from Cloudflare. That skips Cloudflare's protection, and the server also lacks some time limits on slow connections.
example: Someone scanning the internet finds the port and floods it with slow connections; the clinic app becomes unreachable for both clinics during the morning.
why: Easier attacks and outages that Cloudflare would otherwise stop.
fix: Allow port 8443 only from Cloudflare's addresses (or use Cloudflare's origin certificate check) and add read and idle time limits to the server.

title: A few slow reports can freeze the system for everyone
simple: The database connection pool is left at its default of about four connections, with no time limit on queries. Each open live-queue screen also takes a connection of its own.
example: The owner runs a large report while two queue screens are open; the remaining connections are busy, and the cashier's "Collect" button spins for a minute at both clinics.
why: Ordinary work stalls for every clinic at the same time.
fix: Set a proper pool size, a 10-second limit on queries, a time limit per request, and share one connection for all live-queue screens.

title: Test scripts run on the live system with full rights
simple: Some end-to-end test scripts are run against the production system with full database rights. They create test users with a password written in the code, and their clean-up deletes rows across tables with no clinic protection.
example: A bug in the clean-up step matches more than the test rows and deletes real patients at Cure Dental. Test accounts with a publicly known password stay active in production.
why: Real data could be deleted, and known-password accounts left open.
fix: Point these scripts only at a throwaway database and check production for leftover test users.

title: Website lacks standard browser security settings
simple: The site does not send the usual browser security instructions (always use HTTPS, do not allow being framed by other sites, restrict scripts, and so on).
example: A fake site loads the clinic app inside an invisible frame and tricks a receptionist into clicking buttons she cannot see.
why: Easier phishing and some browser-based attacks.
fix: Add the standard security headers in the web server.

title: The app can edit or erase its own history records
simple: The database account the app uses is allowed to change and delete entries in the clinic's history. History should be add-only.
example: A bug, or someone who gets into the server, quietly removes the history line showing who waived a 5,000 birr charge.
why: The history cannot be fully trusted as evidence.
fix: Allow the app only to add history entries, never change or delete them.

title: Clinic database account can change vendor price lists
simple: The database account used for clinic work can also write the vendor's own tables: plans and prices, features, permissions and partner leads. Clinic users cannot reach this through the screens, but a bug could.
example: A bug in a clinic screen updates the plans table and every clinic's limit changes.
why: Vendor-wide settings are not protected from clinic-side mistakes.
fix: Give the clinic account read-only access to vendor tables.

title: Some security steps ignore their own failures
simple: When the system detects a stolen sign-in pass, or a password is reset, it tries to sign the person out everywhere, but if that step fails it carries on silently.
example: A password is reset after a phone is stolen; the "sign out everywhere" step fails because of a database hiccup, nobody is told, and the stolen phone stays signed in.
why: A protection that is believed to have worked may not have.
fix: Treat these steps as must-succeed: retry, and refuse or alert if they fail.

title: Updates go live in clinic hours, untested on a copy
simple: New versions are put live during clinic hours (five times on 2 October), with no test copy of the system to try them on first and only one step of undo.
example: An update at 10:30 has a mistake in the cashier page; Cure Dental cannot take payments until it is undone, with a waiting room full.
why: Each update risks interrupting real clinic work.
fix: Use a test copy, deploy outside clinic hours, and keep more than one previous version to roll back to.

title: A failed update can leave the system half-changed
simple: If a database change or the after-update health check fails, the update stops but nothing is put back automatically. The system can be left half old, half new.
example: A database change fails halfway at 21:00; the app is on the new version, the database on the old one, and patient pages error until someone fixes it by hand.
why: Longer outages after a bad update.
fix: Undo automatically to the previous version (and the pre-update backup if needed) when an update fails.

title: Server logs vanish on every update and are not size-limited
simple: The application logs are lost each time a new version is put live, and are probably not limited in size. The disk is already about 81% full.
example: A clinic reports a strange payment from yesterday; the logs that would explain it disappeared with this morning's update. Meanwhile logs slowly fill the disk until the database stops.
why: Problems cannot be investigated, and a full disk would stop the system.
fix: Keep logs across updates with a size limit and rotation.

title: Test database and another business share the live server
simple: The production server also runs a test database, and another business's software, with no memory limits on that other software.
example: The other business has a busy day and its program uses all the memory; the clinic database is slowed or stopped.
why: Something unrelated to the clinics can take them down.
fix: Move test databases and the other business off the production server, or give them strict memory limits.

title: Background worker gives up if the database is briefly down
simple: If the database is not ready when the background worker starts, it exits instead of retrying, and some failure exits are reported as success, so nothing restarts it properly.
example: After a server reboot the database takes 30 seconds to start; the worker exits, and reminders and history entries stop until someone notices.
why: Silent loss of background work after a restart.
fix: Have the worker retry on start and exit with a failure code when it really fails.

title: A restore can lose a full day of work
simple: Backups run once a night, so restoring after a disaster brings back the state of last night: everything since then is gone.
example: The database is damaged at 16:00; after restoring, the whole day's 40 visits and 60,000 birr of payments must be re-entered from paper.
why: A day's records and payments may have to be re-entered by hand.
fix: Take hourly backups (cheap) or continuous database archiving.
decision: How many hours of lost work can a clinic tolerate?

title: Two-step sign-in exists but staff cannot turn it on
simple: The system has code for a second sign-in step (a phone code), but there is no way for a staff member to set it up.
example: The owner wants the cashier and herself to use a phone code because they handle money; there is no screen to do it.
why: Passwords alone protect patient and money data.
fix: Add a screen to set up and reset the phone-code step, at least for owners and cashiers.

title: Anyone can lock staff out with deliberate wrong passwords
simple: After a few wrong passwords an account is locked for a while. Someone who knows a staff member's email can deliberately type wrong passwords to keep that person locked out.
example: A former employee keeps entering wrong passwords for the cashier's email, and Meron cannot sign in at the start of her shift.
why: Staff can be blocked from working by a nuisance attacker.
fix: Combine the lock with per-address limits and give the owner a quick unlock.

title: AI assistant and voice transcription send patient details outside
simple: The AI assistant and the voice-to-text features send visit details to outside companies (NVIDIA and Deepgram). Patients have not been asked.
example: A dentist uses the assistant on Almaz's visit; her symptoms and history are sent to a company abroad.
why: Patient information leaves the system without consent.
fix: Keep these features off for dental clinics unless the clinic chooses them and patients are informed.
decision: Should these features be available to clinics at all, and if so, with what patient notice?

title: Dashboard and lists do much more database work than needed
simple: Each open dashboard runs about 25 database queries every 30 seconds, some lists are not limited in size, "today" filters cannot use quick lookups, and the whole app downloads as one large file. Fine for two clinics, but it will not scale.
example: With ten clinics each keeping three dashboards open all day, the server is busy answering the same questions over and over and screens become slow.
why: Slower screens and higher server costs as clinics are added.
fix: Combine dashboard queries, limit list sizes, add the missing indexes and split the app into smaller downloads.

title: Some links between records are not enforced by the database
simple: A few tables refer to other records without a database rule making sure the referred record exists, and one common lookup (treatment visits by clinic and date) has no index.
example: A bug leaves a visit pointing at a deleted plan; screens that expect the plan then error.
why: Slow drift into inconsistent data, and slower calendar loading.
fix: Add the missing links and the index.

title: Demo seed passwords are guessable and not blocked in production
simple: The demo data tool sets a default password (ChangeMe123!) and nothing stops it being run against production.
example: Someone runs the demo seed on the live server by mistake; several accounts now have a password anyone could guess.
why: Known-password accounts could appear in production.
fix: Refuse to run the seed in production and require a password to be given explicitly.

title: Old Cloudinary secret copy still on the development computer
simple: Old editor history files on the development computer still contain a Cloudinary secret key that was once leaked.
example: The laptop is lost or shared; whoever has it finds the key and could read or delete files in that Cloudinary account if it was never changed.
why: Patient files in that account could be exposed if the key is still valid.
fix: Confirm the key was replaced in Cloudinary and delete the old history copies.
decision: Was the Cloudinary key rotated after the leak?

title: Allergy written as a plural does not warn on prescriptions
simple: When a prescription is written, the system compares the drug name with the patient's recorded allergies. It only warns if the allergy word appears whole inside the drug name. So an allergy recorded as "Penicillins" (plural) does not warn for "Penicillin V", because "penicillins" is not inside "penicillin v". The same happens for other longer spellings, and the check also does not know drug families (a "Penicillin" allergy only catches Amoxicillin if the clinic's drug list has tagged Amoxicillin as a penicillin).
example: Reception records Almaz's allergy as "Penicillins – severe". Two weeks later Dr Selam prescribes Penicillin V 250 mg for an abscess. No warning appears, the prescription prints, and the only protection left is whether Dr Selam happens to look at the allergy line on the card.
why: A drug the patient is known to react to can be prescribed with no warning, while staff trust that the system would have stopped it. That is a direct patient-harm risk.
fix: Make the match work both ways and ignore simple plural endings (Penicillins = Penicillin), and warn on drug families using the drug list's allergen tags. Add a short list of common families (penicillins, sulfa, NSAIDs) so they are caught even when a drug was typed freely.

log.note: Owner confirmed and chose option A: warn on plurals and spelling variants plus a fixed list of common drug families (penicillins, sulfonamides, NSAIDs and others); keep free typing of the allergy name but suggest the standard names while typing.

Every clinic, existing and new, starts with 26 standard allergy names (suggested as staff type). Four older test rows changed on purpose: aspirin now warns on ibuprofen and penicillin on amoxicillin.
